questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old female presents with fatigue, pallor, and a craving for ice (pagophagia). CBC shows Hb 7.8 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, MCH 20 pg, RDW 18%. Peripheral smear shows microcytic hypochromic red cells with pencil cells. Serum ferritin is 4 ng/mL. Which of the following best describes the expected iron study profile in this patient?

options.A: Low serum iron, low TIBC, high ferritin
options.B: Low serum iron, high TIBC, low ferritin, low transferrin saturation
options.C: Low serum iron, low TIBC, low ferritin
options.D: Normal serum iron, high TIBC, normal ferritin

questions.explanation: Iron deficiency anemia (IDA) is characterized by: low serum iron (reduced stores), high TIBC (body upregulates transferrin production to capture any available iron), low ferritin (ferritin is the most sensitive early marker of iron depletion), and low transferrin saturation (<16%). Pagophagia (ice craving) is a classic pica symptom of IDA. Anemia of chronic disease shows low serum iron but also low TIBC and high/normal ferritin — a key distinguishing feature.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 32-year-old female develops uncontrolled bleeding from IV sites, gum bleeding, and petechiae 12 hours after an abruptio placentae. Lab reports show: PT prolonged, aPTT prolonged, platelet count 42,000/μL, fibrinogen 80 mg/dL, and D-dimer markedly elevated. Peripheral smear shows schistocytes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: DIC is a consumptive coagulopathy triggered by systemic activation of coagulation (here by abruptio placentae releasing tissue factor). Laboratory hallmarks: prolonged PT and aPTT (consumption of clotting factors), thrombocytopenia (platelet consumption), low fibrinogen (<150 mg/dL), markedly elevated D-dimer (fibrin degradation), and schistocytes on smear (microangiopathic hemolytic anemia from fibrin strands shearing RBCs). The triad of bleeding + clotting + thrombocytopenia in an obstetric emergency = DIC until proven otherwise.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old male presents with high-grade fever, gum hypertrophy, bleeding gums, and spontaneous skin ecchymoses. CBC shows WBC 62,000/μL with 80% blasts, Hb 7.2 g/dL, platelets 18,000/μL. Peripheral smear shows blasts with prominent Auer rods. Myeloperoxidase stain is strongly positive. Bone marrow biopsy confirms >30% blasts. Coagulation profile shows low fibrinogen and elevated D-dimer. Which AML subtype is most consistent with this presentation?
questions.explanation: AML M3 (APL) is characterized by: Auer rods (often multiple — 'faggot cells'), strong MPO positivity, life-threatening DIC (due to release of procoagulants from granules), and t(15;17) translocation causing PML-RARα fusion. Gum hypertrophy is more classic of M4/M5 (monocytic), but the DIC and Auer rods here point to M3. Treatment with All-Trans Retinoic Acid (ATRA) differentiates APL blasts and is a medical emergency. Untreated DIC in APL is rapidly fatal.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old male presents with severe back pain, fatigue, and recurrent pneumococcal pneumonia. Investigations show: Hb 8.6 g/dL, serum calcium 12.4 mg/dL, creatinine 2.2 mg/dL, total protein 10.8 g/dL with albumin 3.2 g/dL. Serum protein electrophoresis shows an M-spike in the gamma region. X-ray spine shows multiple lytic lesions and vertebral compression fractures. Bone marrow biopsy shows 40% plasma cells. Urine shows Bence-Jones proteins. Which single investigation is most specific for monitoring treatment response in this patient?

options.B: Serum and urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (M-protein level)
options.C: Bone marrow biopsy repeated at 3 months

questions.explanation: The CRAB criteria confirm Multiple Myeloma: hyperCalcemia, Renal failure, Anemia, Bone lytic lesions. Monoclonal M-protein (paraprotein) quantification by serum/urine electrophoresis and immunofixation is the standard for diagnosis and treatment monitoring — a falling M-spike indicates response. β2-microglobulin is a prognostic marker (staging) not a response marker. Bence-Jones proteinuria (light chains in urine) is characteristic of MM and contributes to cast nephropathy.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old female presents with recurrent epistaxis since childhood, menorrhagia, and prolonged bleeding after a dental extraction. Her sister has a similar history. Investigations show: prolonged bleeding time, prolonged aPTT, normal PT, normal platelet count. Ristocetin cofactor activity is markedly reduced. Factor VIII level is low-normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Von Willebrand Disease (vWD) is the most common inherited bleeding disorder. Type 1 (most common, ~75%) is a quantitative deficiency of vWF. Features: mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, menorrhagia, post-dental bleeding), prolonged bleeding time (platelet plug formation impaired), prolonged aPTT (vWF carries Factor VIII — low vWF leads to low FVIII), normal PT and platelet count, and reduced ristocetin cofactor activity. Autosomal dominant inheritance explains the family history. Hemophilia A has normal bleeding time and affects males.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old male presents with headache, facial plethora, pruritus after a hot shower (aquagenic pruritus), and splenomegaly. CBC shows: Hb 20.2 g/dL, Hct 62%, WBC 14,000/μL, platelets 520,000/μL. Serum erythropoietin is undetectable. JAK2 V617F mutation is detected. What is the most dangerous acute complication this patient is at risk for?

options.C: Arterial and venous thrombosis (stroke, Budd-Chiari syndrome)
options.D: Severe iron deficiency from repeated phlebotomy

questions.explanation: Polycythemia Vera (PV) is a JAK2 V617F-positive myeloproliferative neoplasm causing clonal RBC overproduction. The hallmark symptom is aquagenic pruritus (histamine release from increased basophils). The most serious complication is thrombosis — both arterial (stroke, MI) and venous (Budd-Chiari syndrome, portal vein thrombosis, DVT/PE) — due to hyperviscosity and platelet dysfunction. Budd-Chiari syndrome in a young patient should always prompt JAK2 testing. Treatment: phlebotomy, low-dose aspirin, and hydroxyurea for high-risk patients.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 19-year-old male presents with progressive pallor, spontaneous gum bleeding, and recurrent infections over 3 months. CBC shows: Hb 5.4 g/dL, WBC 1,800/μL (neutrophils 400/μL), platelets 12,000/μL, reticulocyte count 0.1%. Bone marrow biopsy shows hypocellular marrow (<10% cellularity) replaced by fat cells. He has no HLA-matched sibling donor. What is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.A: Allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation from matched unrelated donor

questions.explanation: Severe aplastic anemia (SAA) criteria: marrow cellularity <25%, plus 2 of 3 — neutrophils <500/μL, platelets <20,000/μL, reticulocytes <20,000/μL. For patients without an HLA-matched sibling donor, standard first-line therapy is immunosuppressive therapy (IST) with horse ATG + cyclosporine + eltrombopag (a TPO-receptor agonist that also stimulates HSC recovery). Allogeneic HSCT from a matched sibling is preferred if available and age <40 years. The pathophysiology is T-cell mediated autoimmune destruction of hematopoietic stem cells.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old male receiving a blood transfusion suddenly develops high fever (39.8°C), rigors, flank pain, hemoglobinuria (red-brown urine), and hypotension within 15 minutes of starting the transfusion. The direct Coombs test is positive. What is the most life-threatening immediate complication to anticipate and manage?

options.B: Acute hemolytic transfusion reaction with DIC and acute renal failure
options.C: Febrile non-hemolytic transfusion reaction requiring antipyretics only

questions.explanation: This is an Acute Hemolytic Transfusion Reaction (AHTR), most often caused by ABO incompatibility (clerical error). Complement-mediated intravascular hemolysis causes: fever, rigors, flank/back pain, hemoglobinuria, hypotension/shock. Immediate action: STOP transfusion, maintain IV access, aggressive IV fluids to protect kidneys (target urine output >1 mL/kg/hr), send blood bank repeat crossmatch. Life-threatening complications: DIC (from released RBC stroma activating coagulation) and acute renal failure (from tubular precipitation of free hemoglobin). Positive direct Coombs confirms immune-mediated hemolysis.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old male presents with massive splenomegaly, pancytopenia, and recurrent infections with atypical organisms including Mycobacterium avium. Bone marrow biopsy is a 'dry tap.' Peripheral smear shows cells with abundant pale cytoplasm and irregular cytoplasmic projections ('hairy' cells). TRAP (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase) stain is positive. Flow cytometry is most likely to show which immunophenotype?

options.A: CD5+, CD23+, CD19+, surface IgM dim

questions.explanation: Hairy Cell Leukemia (HCL) is a rare indolent B-cell leukemia. Classic immunophenotype: CD103+ (most specific), CD11c+ (strongly), CD25+, CD19+, CD20+ — the 'CD103, CD11c, CD25, CD123' combination is virtually pathognomonic. TRAP positivity (tartrate-resistant acid phosphatase) is characteristic. BRAF V600E mutation is present in >95%. Bone marrow 'dry tap' occurs due to reticulin fibrosis. Treatment: cladribine (2-CdA) or pentostatin — single course induces durable complete remissions in >80%. CLL shows CD5+/CD23+.

questions.subject: Medicine
questions.question_text: A 3-year-old child is brought with cyanosis and respiratory distress after accidentally ingesting a topical benzocaine teething gel. Pulse oximetry reads 82% but ABG shows PaO2 of 98 mmHg. The blood appears chocolate-brown when drawn. Co-oximetry reveals methemoglobin level of 34%. Which is the correct antidote and its mechanism of action?

options.B: Methylene blue — reduces methemoglobin (Fe³⁺) back to functional hemoglobin (Fe²⁺) via NADPH-methemoglobin reductase
options.C: Hydroxocobalamin — binds free cyanide to form cyanocobalamin
options.D: Sodium thiosulfate — provides sulfur donor for rhodanese enzyme

questions.explanation: Methemoglobinemia occurs when hemoglobin iron is oxidized from Fe²⁺ to Fe³⁺, losing oxygen-carrying capacity and causing a leftward shift of the ODC. Classic clue: cyanosis with normal PaO2 (ABG measures dissolved O2, not Hb-bound) + chocolate-brown blood + SpO2 falsely reading ~85% regardless of true saturation. Antidote: Methylene blue (1-2 mg/kg IV) is reduced by NADPH to leukomethylene blue, which then reduces Fe³⁺ back to Fe²⁺ non-enzymatically. It requires G6PD activity — ineffective/harmful in G6PD deficiency (use ascorbic acid instead). Triggers: benzocaine, dapsone, nitrates, primaquine.
